prompt.context: Our client, the governor of a southeastern state in the US, is worried about student performance in K-12 schools in the state. The state has 180 school districts and recently increased spending from $3.2B to $4.5B annually on public education, but isn't seeing the results it expected. She has hired us to diagnose the problem and identify a solution. We are focused only on public schools — private schools, magnet schools, and charter schools can be ignored. The governor is up for re-election next year and she ran her original campaign on a platform to reimagine education in the state. According to a recent publication, the state ranks 48th in student proficiency.
prompt.question: Diagnose why student achievement has not improved despite the spending increase and recommend a solution. The governor's goal is to increase student achievement.

clarifying_info.q: What metric is used for student proficiency?
clarifying_info.a: Proficiency in mathematics is a good proxy for overall student proficiency.

clarifying_info.q: What does 'Free and Reduced Lunch' mean?
clarifying_info.a: It is the percentage of students who qualify for free or reduced lunch in public schools — typically used as a proxy for poverty in a school district.
These are students learning English as a second language who typically require additional resources to catch up to peers.
Students diagnosed with a physical or mental impairment for whom the state and federal government mandate specific additional resources.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average enrollment size per district?
clarifying_info.a: Average enrollment per district is 800 students.

exhibits.title: Student Demographics and School Funding: National Average vs. Client State
exhibits.shows: A bar chart comparing math proficiency (national average vs. client state) and a table comparing student demographic shares and average per-student funding between the national average and the client state.

exhibits.title: Math Proficiency vs. Proportion of High-Needs Students by District (bubble = enrollment)
exhibits.shows: A scatter plot with proportion of high-needs students on the x-axis (0 to 0.9), math proficiency on the y-axis (0 to 0.8), and bubble size representing enrollment for Districts A through G.

exhibits.title: Math Proficiency vs. Proportion of High-Needs Students by District (bubble = total spend)
exhibits.shows: A scatter plot with proportion of high-needs students on the x-axis, math proficiency on the y-axis, and bubble size representing total spend for Districts A through G.

exhibits.title: Two Proposed Weighted Student Funding Options
exhibits.shows: A table showing two funding allocation options. Option 1 uses a weighted base multiplier per student type. Option 2 uses a flat base amount per student. Note: no change anticipated in the state education budget.

data.note: No change anticipated in state budget for education

framework: Intra-district considerations: student demographics (socioeconomic status, % high-needs), condition of facilities, staffing, age of textbooks
Inter-district considerations: funding disparities across districts, enrollment differences, spending equity relative to student need
Political considerations: what changes can be easily implemented given the election year, key constituents in certain districts, feasibility of reform proposals
Funding analysis: the prompt signals spending increased with no results — must examine whether funds are equitably distributed and whether distribution methodology is flawed

questions.prompt: Analyze Exhibit 1. What does it tell you about the client state vs. the national average?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note: (1) the client state's math proficiency (0.55) is far below the national average (0.713), consistent with ranking 48th; (2) the client state has significantly more high-needs students across all three categories (free/reduced lunch 50% vs 30%; ELL 40% vs 10%; special ed 30% vs 20%); (3) despite higher student need, per-student funding is identical at $13,000. The key insight is that equal funding is NOT equitable given the higher proportion of costly-to-serve students — this should drive toward examining funding distribution.

questions.prompt: Analyze Exhibits 2A and 2B together. What patterns do you observe?
questions.guidance: Exhibit 2A: Districts with higher proportions of high-needs students tend to have lower math proficiency; larger enrollment bubbles cluster toward high-needs/low-proficiency. Candidate should flag potential overcrowding in high-needs districts. Exhibit 2B: High-proficiency districts are spending significantly more per district despite smaller enrollment. Candidate should recall the $13,000 state average from Exhibit 1 and question why certain districts spend so much more — pointing toward inequitable local/state funding distribution. The combined insight should lead the candidate to recommend investigating funding equity.

questions.prompt: Analyze Exhibit 3. The governor is considering two funding options. Calculate the total cost to the state for each option and determine the fiscal impact.
questions.guidance: Candidate must use demographic percentages from Exhibit 1 applied to the average enrollment of 800 students per district and 180 districts. Rounding is not acceptable.

math.setup: Option 1 uses a weighted multiplier on the $13,000 base. Each high-needs category receives additional funding = (weight x $13,000). Students may fall into multiple categories (weights are additive). Use client demographic percentages from Exhibit 1 x 800 to get average enrollment per category per district.
steps: ELL enrollment per district: 800 x 0.40 = 320 students; additional $ per ELL student: 0.1 x $13,000 = $1,300; per-student cost: $13,000 + $1,300 = $14,300; total ELL funding per district: 320 x $14,300 = $4.576M
Free & Reduced Lunch enrollment per district: 800 x 0.50 = 400 students; additional $ per student: 0.2 x $13,000 = $2,600; per-student cost: $15,600; total per district: 400 x $15,600 = $6.240M
Special Education enrollment per district: 800 x 0.30 = 240 students; additional $ per student: 0.4 x $13,000 = $5,200; per-student cost: $18,200; total per district: 240 x $18,200 = $4.368M
Total cost to state (Option 1): $25.584M x 180 districts = $4.605B
Option 2: $31,980 x 800 students x 180 districts = $4.605B; same deficit of $105M
math.answer: Both options cost $4.605B, creating a $105M deficit against the $4.5B state budget. The costs are identical.

questions.prompt: Given the identical deficit under both options, what other considerations should the Governor keep in mind when choosing between them?
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure pros/cons of each option. A matrix/table format is ideal. Option 1 pros: flexible, targets dollars to highest-need students, weights are additive (an ELL student who also qualifies for free lunch gets 30% additional funding), can be iterated over time. Option 1 cons: complex to administer, may be politically difficult to pass. Option 2 pros: simple and easy to understand. Option 2 cons: a flat allocation is inequitable — districts already performing well simply receive more money without targeting need.

brainstorming.prompt: Given that there is a deficit either way — what other considerations should the Governor keep in mind when deciding between the two options?

categories.name: Option 1 — Weighted Formula (Pros)
ideas: Flexible and can be adjusted over time as student demographics change
Schools serving students with the most needs receive the most funding
Weights are additive — a student who is both ELL and on free/reduced lunch gets 30% additional funding, targeting the most vulnerable
Can be iterated and refined as data on outcomes improves

categories.name: Option 1 — Weighted Formula (Cons)
ideas: May be politically difficult to pass — some districts will lose relative funding
Requires agreement on appropriate weight levels

categories.name: Option 2 — Flat Base (Pros)
ideas: Simple and easy to understand for administrators, politicians, and the public
Uniform treatment of all students regardless of district

categories.name: Option 2 — Flat Base (Cons)
ideas: Inequitable — districts that are already performing well will simply receive more money
Does not target funds to students with the greatest need
Misses the insight from the exhibits that high-needs students require proportionally more resources

recommendation: Recommend Option 1 — the weighted student funding formula. Although both options produce the same $105M deficit, Option 1 allocates funds more equitably by directing additional dollars to the students and districts with the greatest need, which is directly tied to the governor's goal of increasing student achievement.
The state should also identify a path to close the $105M funding gap — either by increasing the education budget or phasing in the weighted formula.
risks: Political capital required to change existing funding weights and pass the new formula through the legislature
Some districts that currently receive proportionally more funding may resist the change if their allocations decrease
Complexity of the weighted formula may create implementation and compliance challenges
next_steps: Investigate whether the proposed weights (0.1, 0.2, 0.4) are set at appropriate levels relative to actual incremental cost of serving each student population
Identify other student subgroups that may warrant additional funding (e.g., gifted students, students with chronic absenteeism)
Study the extent to which additional funds actually translate into measurable student achievement improvements
Develop a political strategy for passing the weighted funding formula given the governor's re-election timeline
